Since then, it has undergone several renovation phases to meet modern technical standards, notably in 1948, 1997, 1998, 2006, and 2011. From the beginning, the Royal Theatre has hosted iconic theatre figures such as Sarah Bernhardt and has been the venue for many lyrical and dramatic performances. Today, it offers a varied program including concerts, musicals, comedy shows, and plays. The interior of the theatre is decorated with garnet velvet and gilding, typical of 'Italian-style' halls. The ceiling features panels representing allegories of tragedy, comedy, and vaudeville, as well as the four seasons. A notable work is the painted canvas by Alexandre Obolensky, depicting a trompe-l'œil sky, which guides visitors from the entrance hall to the lower bar. The theatre has an Italian-style auditorium, with wrought-iron balconies, gilded decor, and a ceiling adorned with frescoes.

It can accommodate around 500 spectators.

There is also a richly decorated foyer, often used for receptions, exhibitions, or chamber music concerts.

The cast iron doors of the theatre, created by ironworker Ph-J. Hoyois and decorated by sculptor Émile-Joseph Hoyaux, feature medallions representing Molière, Racine, Grétry, and Roland de Lassus, as well as the coat of arms of the city of Mons.

The theatre has hosted prestigious performances of classical theatre, opera, and ballet. It was both a social and cultural venue.

During World War II, the theatre was briefly closed and used by the German occupiers for propaganda performances.

It has been renovated multiple times, notably in 2003, as part of efforts to enhance Mons’ heritage.

In 2015, it was one of the key venues for Mons European Capital of Culture. Today, the Royal Theatre is a major venue for artistic dissemination:

- Hosts local and international theatre productions.
- Organizes concerts, operas, and dance performances.
- Actively participates in the cultural season of Mars – Mons arts de la scène, which includes several cultural venues in the city.

The Royal Theatre of Mons remains a must-visit for art and culture lovers, offering a unique experience that blends history, architecture, and high-quality performances.
en.Tour Cesar:
The Caesar Tower of Mons is a medieval remnant located in the Château Park, near the belfry. It is one of the few surviving elements of the former Count's Castle of Mons, which served as the residence of the Counts of Hainaut from the 11th to the 15th century.

The Caesar Tower was built in the 13th or 14th century, probably during the reign of John of Avesnes, Count of Hainaut, who undertook a modernization of the castle enclosure at the end of the 13th century. It was located at the northeast end of the castle walls, complementing the Saint-Calixte chapel to the southwest. The entire enclosure measured about 280 meters in perimeter and surrounded an area of approximately 5,000 square meters.

Today, only the base of the Caesar Tower remains visible, integrated into the Château Park, a green space developed in the 19th century on the ruins of the Count's Castle.

In recent decades, efforts have been made to preserve and restore the remnants of the Caesar Tower. Archaeological investigations have been carried out to study its structure and evolution, notably in 2020, in preparation for restoration work aimed at stabilizing the tower and securing the site for visitors.

The Caesar Tower is an important witness to Mons' medieval past and its role as a center of power for the Counts of Hainaut. Though partially in ruins, it remains a significant element of the city's historical heritage.
en.Tour du Val des Ecoliers:
The Tour du Val des Écoliers (Tower of the Scholars' Valley) is a historic defensive tower located in Mons, Belgium. This medieval tower is part of the city's ancient fortifications and stands as a testament to Mons' strategic importance during the Middle Ages.

Built in the 14th century, the tower was part of the defensive system that protected the city of Mons. It is named after the nearby Val des Écoliers (Scholars' Valley), which was historically associated with educational institutions and religious communities.

The tower features typical medieval military architecture with thick stone walls, narrow windows designed for archers, and a solid construction meant to withstand attacks. Its strategic location allowed it to serve as both a defensive position and a lookout point for monitoring the surrounding area.

Today, the Tour du Val des Écoliers is a protected historical monument that contributes to Mons' rich architectural heritage. While it may not be open to the public for regular visits, it remains an important landmark that helps visitors understand the city's medieval past and its evolution from a fortified settlement to a modern urban center.

The tower serves as a reminder of Mons' historical role as a strategic military and administrative center in the region, and its preservation helps maintain the connection between the city's past and present.
en.Tour Valenciennoise:
The Tour Valenciennoise (Valenciennes Tower) is a historic defensive tower located in Mons, Belgium. This medieval tower is part of the city's ancient fortifications and stands as a testament to Mons' strategic importance during the Middle Ages.

Built in the 14th century, the tower was part of the defensive system that protected the city of Mons. It is named after the city of Valenciennes, which was historically an important administrative and military center in the region. The tower served as a key defensive position along the city's fortifications.

The tower features typical medieval military architecture with thick stone walls, narrow windows designed for archers, and a solid construction meant to withstand attacks. Its strategic location allowed it to serve as both a defensive position and a lookout point for monitoring the surrounding area.

Today, the Tour Valenciennoise is a protected historical monument that contributes to Mons' rich architectural heritage. While it may not be open to the public for regular visits, it remains an important landmark that helps visitors understand the city's medieval past and its evolution from a fortified settlement to a modern urban center.

The tower serves as a reminder of Mons' historical role as a strategic military and administrative center in the region, and its preservation helps maintain the connection between the city's past and present.
en.Tresors de Sainte Waudru:
The Treasures of Sainte Waudru are a remarkable collection of religious artifacts and precious objects housed in the Collegiate Church of Sainte-Waudru in Mons. This exceptional treasury represents centuries of devotion, artistic craftsmanship, and the rich religious heritage of the city.

The collection includes numerous precious objects dating from the Middle Ages to the present day, including reliquaries, liturgical vessels, vestments, and works of art. Among the most notable pieces are the reliquary of Sainte Waudru, containing the remains of the city's patron saint, and various objects used in religious ceremonies throughout the centuries.

The treasury also houses a collection of liturgical vestments, some of which are several centuries old and represent the finest examples of textile art from different periods. These vestments are still used during special religious ceremonies, particularly during the Ducasse de Mons celebrations.

Many of the objects in the treasury are made of precious materials such as gold, silver, and precious stones, reflecting the importance of the Collegiate Church as a center of religious and cultural life in Mons. The collection also includes works by renowned artists and craftsmen from different periods.

The Treasures of Sainte Waudru are not only of religious significance but also represent an important part of Mons' cultural heritage. They provide visitors with insight into the artistic and religious traditions that have shaped the city's identity over the centuries.

The treasury is carefully preserved and maintained, ensuring that these precious objects continue to be available for future generations to appreciate and study. Access to the treasury may be limited to guided tours or special occasions, allowing for proper conservation of these delicate and valuable artifacts.
en.Collegiale Sainte Waudru:
The Collegiate Church of Sainte-Waudru is one of the most magnificent religious buildings in Mons, Belgium, and a masterpiece of Gothic architecture. This imposing church, dedicated to the city's patron saint, Sainte Waudru, stands as a testament to the religious and cultural importance of Mons throughout the centuries.

Construction of the collegiate church began in the 15th century and continued over several centuries, resulting in a magnificent example of Brabant Gothic architecture. The church features soaring vaulted ceilings, intricate stone carvings, and magnificent stained glass windows that create an atmosphere of spiritual grandeur.

The church houses numerous artistic treasures, including the famous Car d'Or (Golden Chariot), a magnificent processional carriage used during the Ducasse de Mons celebrations. The treasury contains precious reliquaries, liturgical objects, and works of art that reflect the church's rich history and the devotion of generations of worshippers.

The Collegiate Church of Sainte-Waudru is particularly famous for its association with the Ducasse de Mons, the city's most important folk festival. During this annual celebration, the relics of Sainte Waudru are carried through the streets of Mons in the Car d'Or, following a tradition that dates back to the 14th century.

The church's architecture and artistic treasures make it a must-visit destination for anyone interested in religious art, medieval architecture, or the cultural heritage of Mons. The building continues to serve as an active place of worship while also welcoming visitors who come to admire its beauty and learn about its history.

The Collegiate Church of Sainte-Waudru is not just a religious building but a living symbol of Mons' identity and a testament to the city's enduring faith and cultural traditions.
en.Ancien Chateau Comtal:
The Ancien Château Comtal (Old Count's Castle) is a historic site in Mons that represents the medieval origins of the city. Although the castle itself no longer exists, the site where it once stood is of great historical and archaeological significance.

The castle was originally built in the 11th century and served as the residence of the Counts of Hainaut, who ruled over the region during the Middle Ages. It was strategically located on a hill overlooking the city, providing both protection and a symbol of the count's authority over the territory.

The castle complex included defensive walls, towers, living quarters, and administrative buildings. It was the center of political and military power in the region, and many important historical events took place within its walls. The castle also housed the chapel of Saint-Calixte, which still exists today and is one of the oldest religious buildings in Mons.

Over the centuries, the castle fell into disrepair and was eventually demolished. However, archaeological excavations have revealed important information about the castle's layout and the daily life of its inhabitants. The site continues to be of interest to historians and archaeologists studying the medieval history of Mons.

Today, the site of the Ancien Château Comtal is part of the Beffroi de Mons UNESCO World Heritage site. Visitors can see the remains of the castle's foundations and the chapel of Saint-Calixte, which provides a tangible connection to Mons' medieval past.

The Ancien Château Comtal represents an important chapter in Mons' history, serving as a reminder of the city's origins as a fortified settlement and its evolution into the modern city it is today.
en.Anciens Abattoirs:
The Anciens Abattoirs (Old Slaughterhouses) of Mons are historic industrial buildings that represent an important part of the city's economic and social history. These buildings, constructed in the 19th century, served as the main slaughterhouse facility for the city of Mons and the surrounding region.

The slaughterhouses were built to meet the growing demand for meat processing in the rapidly industrializing city. They were designed with practical considerations in mind, including proper drainage, ventilation, and facilities for the various stages of meat processing. The buildings reflect the industrial architecture of the period, with functional design taking precedence over aesthetic considerations.

The facility played an important role in the local economy, providing employment for many residents and ensuring a safe and regulated meat supply for the city. The slaughterhouses operated for many decades, serving the needs of the growing population of Mons and the surrounding area.

As the city modernized and food processing methods changed, the old slaughterhouses became obsolete and were eventually closed. However, the buildings remain as a testament to Mons' industrial heritage and the evolution of food processing technology.

Today, the Anciens Abattoirs are protected as part of Mons' industrial heritage. While they may not be open to the public for regular visits, they serve as an important reminder of the city's economic development and the role that industrial facilities played in shaping the urban landscape.

The preservation of these buildings helps maintain a connection to Mons' industrial past and provides valuable insight into how the city's economy and infrastructure have evolved over time.
en.Square:
Tucked away in the historic center of Mons, just a stone’s throw from the Grand-Place and the Belfry, Square Saint-Germain is a small, charming green space that’s full of character. 

Set on the former site of the Saint-Germain Collegiate Church—demolished during the French Revolution—this public garden tells part of the city’s long and layered story. 

The square was designed in 1887 by architects Joseph Hubert and Louis Fuchs, and has been renovated several times since, most recently between 2017 and 2021. Today, it offers a harmonious blend of old-world charm and modern comfort, with redesigned paths, updated urban furniture, inviting benches, and the shade of a majestic chestnut tree. 

A highlight of the square is its commemorative fountain dedicated to the Mons volunteers of the 1830 Belgian Revolution. Originally located on Place Régnier-au-Long-Col, it was moved here in 1930 to mark the centenary of the event. Quiet and dignified, the fountain honors the city’s enduring spirit of freedom and resilience. 

Far more than a shortcut or meeting point, Square Saint-Germain is now a true “urban oasis,” beloved by locals and visitors alike. 

Whether you're looking to take a peaceful break, enjoy a bit of greenery, or simply soak in the atmosphere, this hidden gem offers a welcome pause in the heart of the city.
en.Pilori:
Nestled at the foot of the majestic Sainte-Waudru Collegiate Church, on the quiet Place du Chapitre, stands an elegant and little-known fountain: the Pilori Fountain. 

Built in 1779 at the request of the church chapter, it replaced an older well that dated back to the 16th century. 

Designed by the architect Ouvertus, the fountain features a refined triangular shape in Louis XVI style, made from local blue limestone from Écaussinnes. 

Delicately sculpted pilasters frame the structure, which is topped by a slender pyramid, a decorative vase, and a banner bearing the chapter’s coat of arms—symbols of its ecclesiastical heritage. 

Unlike many purely decorative fountains, this one was fully functional, fed by an ancient aqueduct from the Lafond spring, and served as a valuable water source for the neighborhood. 

Classified as a historical monument in 1955, the fountain has been restored several times over the years to preserve its beauty and original details. 

Today, it remains one of the few 18th-century fountains still standing in Mons. 

Discreet and refined, the Pilori Fountain blends beautifully with the Gothic grandeur of Sainte-Waudru. It offers a striking contrast between medieval stone and 18th-century ornamentation—an evocative reminder of the city’s rich civic and religious heritage.
en.Rue Cronque:
Few streets in Mons wear their name so well. In the local speech, “cronque” means winding, askew, twisted. The street goes nowhere in a straight line: it bends, slips away, refuses the grid of the main roads.

That is why VisitMons put it on its trail of unusual places. In the cobbles, a cross is drawn — discreet, almost secret. Walk too fast and you miss it. No one quite agrees on what it means: a boundary mark, a sign of devotion, the ghost of an older layout? The mystery belongs to the place.

Beyond the bends, the street leads toward the castle park, Saint-Calixte chapel and the belfry. You leave the obvious city for a Mons that hides. Look up at the narrow façades, then down at the stones: the cross is there, somewhere under your feet.
en.Rue à Degrés:
Rue à Degrés is not a street in the usual sense: it is a staircase. Short, steep, tucked into the Rachot quarter, it escapes anyone who sticks to the main axes. The name says exactly what it is — steps, degrees, a climb you scale rather than stroll.

Today a spectacular mural by Nevercrew, a Swiss street-art duo, has turned the walls into a vertical ocean. A huge whale seems to dissolve against the stone: the work is called Dissipation. The contrast is deliberate. A medieval alley, a creature of the deep, a trompe-l’œil that plays with the slope.

This is precisely the kind of place a visitor does not discover alone. Climb, descend, find the angle from which the whale looks most real. The street is brief; the image stays.
en.Ruelle du Cerf Blanc:
The name suggests a sign, a heraldic animal, perhaps a vanished inn. In old imagery the white stag is a rare, almost magical creature — not something you meet on the high road.

Neither is this alley. Tucked into the Parc district, it slips past the tourist flow. Yet VisitMons lists it among the quarter’s curiosities: 17th-century houses here are protected as monuments. Brick and stone, modest volumes, steep roofs: Mons before the 19th-century breakthroughs.

Step in quietly. The lane is narrow, domestic, almost private. Nothing shouts. That is what makes it precious: a scrap of urban fabric the city kept, and that you find only by getting a little lost.
en.Cour du Noir Lévrier:
Greyhounds have a long memory in Mons. On the Grand-Place, the house Au Blanc Lévrier shows two stone dogs. Here it is the opposite: a black greyhound, a courtyard, a name that sounds like an old trade sign or inn.

The Cour du Noir Lévrier is not a street. It is a pocket, a hollow in the block, a paved close that the façades conceal. It has long figured in Mons topography and was carefully refurbished — enough to walk through, not enough to turn it into scenery.

The secret here is architectural. Nothing on the main street says a miniature world opens behind. Go to the end. Listen to footsteps on the cobbles. This is the Mons you miss, and do not forget once found.
en.Chateau de le Marcote:
On the axis, above the ground floor, a limestone panel in the shape of a truncated mitre, set in the brick. At the top, widely spaced: 1689, a horizontal stroke. In the centre, a relief: three weasels in profile, running from left to right, one behind the other. Under the motif, two lines in capitals: LE CHATEAU DE, then LE MARCOTE. At the very bottom, smaller: RECONSTRUIT EN 1820.

The year at the top is that of the stone. The last line, an addition, says the dwelling was rebuilt. On the same limestone one therefore reads the date of the sign and that of the nineteenth-century works.

Address: Rue des Marcottes 33, 7000 Mons.
en.Rue des Fillettes:
Rue des Fillettes: it sounds like a dolls’ lane, a name for children. It is not. In Ancien Régime Mons, the “fillettes” here were the women who worked as prostitutes in this quarter — a trade that was regulated, taxed, and written into the town’s papers.

A municipal document of 1543 already mentions the street. VisitMons does not dodge the point: the name keeps the memory of a Mons less smooth than its collegiate churches. The pleasure quarter was not hidden outside the walls; it was part of the urban fabric, within reach of the Grand-Place.

Today’s line is modest. Once the way counted for more in inner traffic. Walking it, you tread a toponym that was never cleaned up. The people of Mons kept the word. It is for you to hear what it really says.
en.Rue de la Voussure:
Voussure: in architecture, the curve of a vault, the inner face of an arch. It is a rare word on a street sign. In Mons it names a passage that once ran under the church of Saint-Germain — a pious tunnel, a shortcut of shadow between two streets.

Saint-Germain has vanished from the skyline as we know it, but the street kept the name of what passed beneath. The path inventory gives it barely fifty metres. That is little. It is enough to imagine the stone arch, the faithful walking through, the cold of the vault.

Today the sky is open. What remains is the riddle of the name, and a tiny alignment. Look for the narrowest point, a change of level, anything that still betrays a passage under a building. The vault is gone; the word did not yield.
en.Cour de l'Âne Barré:
The barred donkey is not a donkey in jail. “Barré”, for the animal, means a dark band running down its back from mane to tail — a natural St Andrew’s cross, common on some donkeys. The sign, like so many in Mons, stuck to the street.

The courtyard still exists in the street register. It opens a few paces from the Grand-Place, and in three strides you change century: fewer terraces, more cobbles, an inn’s name on the walls. A business still uses the name, proof the toponym is not dead.

Why a donkey so near municipal power? Because talking signs — greyhounds, stags, donkeys, apples — were the GPS of the unlettered. You met “at the Barred Donkey”. Step into the court. The name is enough; the hush of the urban pocket does the rest.
en.Chasse du Bon Dieu:
Forget the hunt. In Mons a chasse is an alley, a gulley between houses, too narrow to be called a street. The word belongs to the old plot vocabulary, like “rampe” or “cour”. The Chasse du Bon Dieu is among the most secret.

The nickname is not a random pious joke. In this area stood a Christ of Pity, the “Bon Dieu de Pitié” — a sorrowful Christ, often seated, crowned with thorns, prayed to in passing. Such popular images lined the streets; some gave their name to the way.

Today the chasse is tiny, almost a threshold. You cross it in a few steps. That is enough to understand Mons before the boulevards: a city of folds, shortcuts and religious signs set at the corners of walls. Look for the quiet. It is the real monument.
en.Cour du Bailly:
The bailiff was the prince’s officer, the arm of justice and administration. In the 16th century, texts speak of a lane of the bailiff of Soignies, slipped between gardens and houses, at the back of the old comital castle. The Cour du Bailly is its heir.

It was not a dead end. Medieval ways connected, pierced, linked the castle to the gardens and the gardens to the town. Time closed some outlets; the name remained, with its floating spelling — Bailly, bailli.

You are in a Mons of power, but backstage: not the Grand-Place, not the collegiate church, the underside of the castle. Courts like this were spaces of service, of passage, sometimes of quiet prestige. Walk to the end; imagine the lost way through to the gardens. The Middle Ages are not always monumental; sometimes they fit in a courtyard.
en.Rampe Sainte Waudru:
The rampe Sainte-Waudru is not just a way up to the collegiate church. It is the stage of a living belief. Every Trinity Sunday, the Car d’Or — the 18th-century processional wagon that carries the shrine of Saint Waudru — must climb this cobbled slope in one go.

Tradition is blunt: if the horses, the crowd and the pushers do not bring the wagon to the top without stopping, misfortune will hit Mons that year. So hundreds of hands throw themselves on the shafts. This is not postcard folklore; it is a joyful, collective anxiety, renewed each year.

The legend is rooted in the plague of 1349, when the saint’s relics were brought out. The ramp itself makes the effort visible: the lower town hauls its treasure toward the high church. Climb it on foot. Measure the slope. Imagine six horses, a gilded wagon, and the ban on stopping.
en.Rampe du Château:
Before the Baroque belfry there was the castle of the counts of Hainaut. The rampe du Château is its topographic memory: a short, paved climb, stuck to the relief of the “Catiau”. You do not drive it; you climb it, as you would a last defence.

With rue des Clercs and rue des Gades it forms a triangle of narrow streets, old façades and sudden views of the tower. This is the belfry’s secret Mons, the one you miss if you stay on the esplanade.

The official register confirms the thoroughfare. Nothing anecdotal: this fold of ground is why the upper town exists. Below, trade; above, power. The ramp is the joint. Pause halfway: the belfry tilts, roofs stack, and you see why Mons was built in layers.
en.Rue des Gades:
Gades: goats. The word survived on the plate while it retreated from conversation. Like cronque, like agache (the magpie), it belongs to the Mons dialect. No one keeps goats at the foot of the belfry now, but the street remembers.

Why goats here? A talking sign, old pasture on the castle slopes, a resident’s nickname: three hypotheses circulate, and that is all to the good. Mons’s animal street names — goats, doe, greyhound, stag, donkey — sketch a town that named its streets as one names an inn.

The street is short, historic, tied to the Clercs–Château knot. Look up: the belfry springs between two gables. This is not a postcard route; it is vocabulary in the open air. Say “gades” out loud. The word tastes of cobble.
en.Rue des Cinq Visages:
Five faces. The name is a delightful trap. Sculptures on a façade? A vanished sign? Five stone heads now lost? Hypotheses crowd in, and no explanatory plaque kills the mystery — lucky, for an unusual street.

What we know better is the geography. The street clings to the quarter of Sainte-Waudru and roughly follows an old medieval enclosure. Mons belted itself in stone more than once; each wall left folds, edge-streets, leftover names.

Walk slowly. Count windows, mascarons, keystones. You may find fewer than five faces, or more. The wall itself shows only as relief, a break in the building line, a memory of a ditch. The name is enough to make you look. That is already a great deal.
en.Rue de la Grosse Pomme:
The Fat Apple: another sign, another name that makes you smile before you think. In Ancien Régime towns an apple — fat, golden, or simply a fruit — marked an inn, a house, a meeting place. The word migrated from the façade to the street, and stayed.

But this lane is more than a tasty toponym. It runs by Sainte-Waudru and belonged to the traditional procession route. The Car d’Or, the shrines, the pious crowd: all of that used these metres of cobble. The relief, besides, keeps the memory of a medieval wall — a drop, a remnant of masonry, the edge of the upper town.

So you stand at once in a vanished inn, on a ritual path, and on an old military frontier. Three Mons on one plate. Taste the name, then the slope.
en.Rue de la Peine Perdue:
Rue de la Peine Perdue. It sounds like a novel title, or the moral of a fable. It is a real street, next to Saint-Elisabeth, in the current register of Mons thoroughfares.

Where does the phrase come from? “Peine perdue” means wasted effort. People have suggested a building site that never finished, a passage too narrow for trade, a lawsuit, a house too costly to realign. As so often with savoury street names, learned etymology stops at the edge of folklore. The name pleased; it was kept.

The mood is anything but wasted. Old Mons, a Baroque-and-Gothic church close by, a lane that does not open on the usual tourist map. Read the plate aloud. Passers-by will smile. You will be exactly where you should be: in a city unashamed of its odd words.
en.Rue des Trois Boudins:
The Three Black Puddings are not a carnival legend. The street is on the register, behind the Mundaneum — Otlet and La Fontaine’s “paper Google”. On one side, the dream of classifying all the world’s knowledge; on the other, three boudins. Mons lives with the mix.

The name most likely comes from a sign. Food trades — tripe sellers, pork butchers — displayed their goods. Three puddings, clearly visible, were as good as a house number. You met there. When the signs came down, the streets sometimes kept the menu.

Look up at the back of the Mundaneum: brick, verticality, a hint of Amsterdam School expressionism. Then read the plate again. The learned and the tasty share the same enclave. A lesson in toponymy, and an excellent reason to smile.
en.Rampe Borgnagache:
Borgnagache. The word resists a first reading. Two traditions fight over its origin, which suits an unusual ramp.

The first is dialect: agasse, agache, the magpie — black and white, talkative, a thief in the proverbs. “Borgne agache” could mean the one-eyed magpie, or a particular bird, again a sign. The second is onomastic: Jean and Jacques Borgnagache are said to have founded a hospital in the quarter. The rare family name would have slid onto the slope.

Both stories can live together: people sometimes wear bird names. The ramp itself is concrete — a climb, a fold of old Mons, a word more often photographed than spoken. Try it. Borg-na-gache. Somewhere, the magpie is still laughing.
en.Ruelle aux Quinettes:
Quinettes means almost nothing, which is why you stop. Local scholars see a distortion of Hocquinette — a surname, an owner, a house that named the alley. Spelling slipped, pronunciation followed, and we were left with quinettes, like a child’s word.

The Rachot quarter is a maze. This lane is among the most intimate: too narrow for ceremony, too short for hurried guides. It is a spelling mistake that became a landscape.

Mons is full of such slides. Cronque, gades, quinettes: spoken language sculpts the map. Stepping in, you are not visiting a monument; you are visiting a rumour written on a plate.
en.Rue de la Petite Guirlande:
The Little Garland: the word smells of fairground and liturgy. Garlands dressed the streets on procession days; a sign, a recurring decoration, a quarter’s nickname may have frozen into the toponym. Towns sometimes have a Great and a Little of the same thing — here the little one survived.

Above all, the street is not a footnote in the Mons calendar. It remains on the traditional route of the Car d’Or procession, the cortège that, in principle since the 14th century, carries Saint Waudru through the town. So this is not only a pretty name: it is a stretch of ritual.

Away from the Grand-Place’s noise, the garland is a linking street, quieter, turned toward the west and the station. On Ducasse day it remembers it is a theatre. On other days it waits, with its feast-day name.
en.Rue de l'Âtre:
The âtre is the hearth, the blackened stone where the fire is made. To give that name to a street is to speak of warmth, of home, perhaps of a sign “At the Hearth”, or a place where people huddled in winter. In a stone city, the word warms.

The neighbourhood explains the rest. Saint-Nicolas-en-Havré, the first parish outside the walls (1224), has a sorrowful Christ on a side façade — another of those roadside “bons dieux” the people of Mons greeted in passing. Rue de l’Âtre and that Christ belong to the same devout, domestic Mons, the Mons of everyday gestures rather than great ceremonies.

Look at the church, then the street. Monumental Baroque on one side; on the other, a word of kitchen and vigil. That is the whole town: the sacred stuck to the saucepan.
en.Rue de la Terre du Prince:
The Prince’s Land: the name speaks of property. Before it was a street it was soil, a tenure, a piece of the counts of Hainaut’s domain. The prince here is no fairy tale; he is the feudal power that held the castle, the gardens, the warren, and the ground at the foot of the walls.

Most interesting, for anyone hunting invisible Mons, are the remains of the enclosure. Mons had several belts of stone. In this sector the wall — sometimes called Baldwin’s — still shows: a facing, a drop, a scar in the plots. The street runs along an old frontier.

So you walk a selvage. On one side, the burghers’ town; on the other, once, the prince. Look up at what is left of the fortification. The street’s name is not poetic by accident: it is legal, military, and very concrete.
en.Rue des Quatre Fils Aymon:
The Four Sons of Aymon are not a Mons family. They are the heroes of a chanson de geste: four brothers — Renaud de Montauban and his younger siblings — hunted by Charlemagne, saved by the fairy horse Bayard, who could carry all four at once. The tale ran through northern Europe; in Mons it landed on a street sign.

Why here? Chivalric romances fed inn signs and street names. An inn “At the Four Sons of Aymon”, a literary fashion, an owner fond of epic: the name stuck, and the discreet street kept it.

The buildings deserve a pause. At number 6, stained glass and a careful door; at 14, the monumental portal of a former private hôtel. This is no anonymous lane. It is a legend stuck to fine stone. Look for Bayard in a fanlight, a piece of ironwork, a memory. Even absent, the horse still gallops in the name.
en.Rue des Clercs:
Clerks were people of writing and of the Church: copyists, chaplains, officers of the chapter. A rue des Clercs, at the foot of the castle and the collegiate church, tells of a town where power could read, pray and count.

Today one comes for the landscape. The street coils under the belfry, offers unexpected glimpses of El Catiau, and lines up a tight Mons heritage — first among them the Spanish House, brick Gothic, now the UNESCO Heritage House. Nothing is wide; everything is dense.

This is backstage Mons. You leave the Grand-Place, you dive in, and the Baroque tower appears over a stepped gable. Take time to look up at every number. Rue des Clercs is not a shortcut: it is a cabinet of curiosities in the open air, if you walk slowly.
en.Rue des Sœurs Grises:
Mons was a city of convents. Black sisters, grey sisters, Visitandines, canonesses of Sainte-Waudru: the medieval and early-modern plan is punctured with cloisters, chapels, enclosures. Rue des Sœurs Grises is a surviving toponym.

The Grey Sisters, often Franciscan tertiaries, were set apart by the colour of their habit — ash grey, humbler than the black of the Augustinian hospitaliers. They nursed, begged, sometimes taught. When the Revolution and later regimes emptied the convents, the streets kept the nicknames.

A few steps away, the street and convent of the Black Sisters tell the same story in counterpoint. Here there is no great cloister to photograph; a name, a current thoroughfare, a memory of cloth. Read both plates on the same day. You will have the Mons of women in religion, the one hurried guides too quickly reduce to Sainte-Waudru.
en.Rue du 11 novembre:
You leave the Doudou museum through the back of the Hôtel de Ville and find yourself on Rue du 11 novembre. The name commemorates the armistice of 11 November 1918: Mons, occupied from August 1914, was liberated on the last day of the Great War by the Canadian Corps.

The street is short, a passageway between the Mayeur garden and the museum district. Behind you, the Doudou; in front of you, the city reclaiming its streets.

Continue towards Rue Neuve. At number 8, the CAP museum, the City collections, opens its doors. This is the next stop, before heading along Rue d'Enghien towards the belfry and the collegiate church.

Address: Rue du 11 novembre, 7000 Mons.
en.Rue Neuve:
Rue Neuve leads to the museum heart of Mons. At number 8, the CAP museum — Museum of the Collections — presents the City’s permanent collections: ancient, modern and contemporary art, in a thematic route.

The glass building, set on pillars, dialogues with the old façades of the centre. The BAM, right next door, hosts temporary exhibitions; the CAP, meanwhile, preserves the Mons collection, the one you come back to see.

If the museum is open, a visit completes the Doudou: on one side living folklore, on the other art collections. Then continue towards Rue d'Enghien, the belfry and the collegiate church.

Address: Rue Neuve 8, 7000 Mons.
en.Rue d'Enghien:
Rue d’Enghien links the shopping centre to the castle district. You take it after Rue Neuve, descending towards the collegiate church of Sainte-Waudru, the belfry and the Château park.

It is a connecting street, narrow, slightly sloping. At number 19, the fresco Instant suspendu by Laurence Vray freezes a gesture on the wall: a still image between the Grand-Place and the belfry.

Further on, Rue Cronque takes over, even more winding. You leave the museums behind for the Mons of stone and cobblestones.

Address: Rue d'Enghien, 7000 Mons.
en.Rue du Chapitre:
Rue du Chapitre takes its name from the institution that shaped Mons as much as the Hôtel de Ville: the chapter of the canonesses of Sainte-Waudru. Noble ladies, they prayed, managed lands and held rank in the city.

The street links the collegiate church to Saint-Germain square. You can still feel the cloister nearby: doors, gardens, silence a little apart from the Grand-Place.

Look up at the volumes of blue stone and brick. You are in canonical Mons, that of the holy foundress, before heading back down towards the shopping streets.

Address: Rue du Chapitre, 7000 Mons.
en.Rue des Fripiers:
Rue des Fripiers owes its name to the second-hand clothes merchants: garments, sheets, used fabrics. In the Middle Ages and under the Ancien Régime, each trade had its own street; this one kept the second-hand textile trade, very close to the Grand-Place.

Today it is one of the liveliest shopping streets in the centre. Old façades, shop windows, and beneath your feet painted cobblestones that have made the rounds on social media.

You will find THANKSgalerie here, Lask’Art, and further on Rue de la Coupe. Stroll along: the Mons of shops begins here.

Address: Rue des Fripiers, 7000 Mons.
en.Thanks Galerie:
At 22 Rue des Fripiers, THANKSgalerie occupies one of the oldest façades on the street, dated 1606. Behind this stone, a contemporary space: exhibitions, sales, meetings.

Created in 2015 by Benoît Dumortier, the gallery first travelled before settling here in March 2022, in a venue designed with the Maison du Design. More than thirty exhibitions, thousands of visitors: it has found its place in one of the liveliest streets in the centre.

If the door is open — Wednesday afternoons, Friday and Saturday, or by appointment — go in. Otherwise, look at the façade: 1606 outside, today’s art inside.

Address: Rue des Fripiers 22, 7000 Mons.
en.Lask'Art:
At 32 Rue des Fripiers, Lask’Art is part of the string of galleries and shops that make this street a place for strolling as much as for shopping.

Mons loves art in the street and art behind the window. Here, creation is shown at passer-by height: you stop, you look, you push the door open if the place is open.

After THANKSgalerie, this is a second artistic stop before heading to Rue de la Coupe and, further on, the Grand-Place.

Address: Rue des Fripiers 32, 7000 Mons.
en.Rue de la Coupe:
Rue de la Coupe probably owes its name to a sign: the cup, the ciborium, the vessel. At the address where you can still see À la Coupe d’Or, a stone ciborium recalls the goldsmiths’ trades and the taverns of old Mons.

It is a short street, a link between the Fripiers, the Grand-Place and the Coupe district. People pass through it more than they linger there — unfairly.

Look up. Stone signs are the comic strip of commerce in days gone by. This one, golden in name, then leads you back to the Grand-Place, the end of the family route.

Address: Rue de la Coupe, 7000 Mons.
en.Lola Goies Rue du Miroir:
You are discovering “Lola Goies”, a work from the L'Art habite la Ville programme, created by Lola Goies, a student at ARTS² in Belgium. On Rue du Miroir, she offers a dragon that wanders through the city at night. The motif enters into dialogue with the mirror theme and with the Ducasse de Mons, as requested in the project.

This mural comes from a collaboration between the ARTS² drawing students and the Urban Arts Committee initiated by the City. The drawing plays with the idea of a discreet apparition. It appears, then disappears, like a creature observing Mons without ever really being caught.

Address: Rue du Miroir 18, 7000 Mons.
en.Laurence Vray Instant suspendu:
You are in front of “Instant suspendu,” a work from the L'Art habite la Ville program, by Laurence Vray, an artist from Mons, Belgium. At Rue d'Enghien, 19, she offers an image that speaks of intimacy, water and lightness. Here, photography becomes a pause, almost a breath in the middle of the journey.

Laurence Vray’s work explores the resonances of water, its currents and flows. The VisitMons text emphasizes the oppositions she stages: presence and absence, solitude and companionship, fragility and strength. This work moves with restraint and creates a discreet emotion, but one that is very present.

Address: Rue d'Enghien 19, 7000 Mons.
en.Eva Badalamenti Passage de l'ilot:
Here is “Eva Badalamenti,” a work from the L'Art habite la Ville program, created by Eva Badalamenti, a young student at ARTS² in Belgium. In the Passage de l'Îlot, the mural accompanies your walk and turns this passageway into a place to stop. It highlights the presence of a young Mons-based creative talent at the heart of the city.

The VisitMons text presents Eva as a talented student at Arts². The work is therefore part of a dynamic of training and visibility for urban art. Here, the place is not merely crossed. It becomes a medium for expression and part of an artistic route.

Address: Passage de l'Îlot, 7000 Mons.
en.Atelier Pica Pica Panorama:
Atelier Pica Pica brings together Boris Magotteaux, Manuel Falcata and Jérome Degive. The work invites you to look at Mons differently, seeking in the forms and shadows what belongs to the city itself. The passage then becomes a space for reading, almost a small mural theatre stage.

Address: Passage Victor Hugo, 7000 Mons.
en.Hell'O Folks:
It diverts mystic-esoteric symbols and combines them with cartoon and comic-book figures.

Hell’O, with Jérôme Meynen and Antoine Detaille, comes from the graffiti world. Here, the duo sets aside lettering to work with paper, painting, ink drawing, and installation. The work also draws on the theme of the Doudou and presents a mural that is vibrant, luminous, and deliberately unsettling.

Address: Rue du 11 Novembre 8, 7000 Mons.
en.Kobra Torre de Saber:
With “Torre de Saber”, Kobra creates a monumental mural in Rue du Mont du Parc. The title evokes a tower of knowledge, and the image gives the city a strong, almost symbolic presence. This work is part of the “L’Art habite la Ville” programme, and it accompanies your walk through Mons.

Here, the wall becomes a visual landmark. Kobra likes very large formats and compositions that seem in motion, with bold colours and dynamic lines. In front of this piece, you can see how urban art can transform a simple passage into a meeting point between the city, the artist’s gesture, and your own gaze.

Address: Rue du Mont du Parc, 7000 Mons
en.Zesar Bahamonte Saint Georges:
With “Saint-Georges”, Zësar Bahamonte, an artist from Spain, creates a mural on rue du Grand Jour, at number 29. This work is part of the “L’Art habite la Ville” program. It takes up the figure of Saint George, known in several traditions, and brings him into the urban landscape of Mons.

The artist explains that he has known this character for a long time, through other artists, painters and musicians. Here, he chooses to work on a theme that speaks to the culture of a place, its history and its inhabitants. The savior saint facing the dragon becomes a strong image, easy to read, yet rich in meaning.

This mural also speaks to you about connection and transmission. It shows how a legend can travel across countries, eras and cultures, while keeping its power in the street.

Address: Rue du Grand Jour 29, 7000 Mons
en.Arts2 Tunnel de la Paix:
With “Tunnel de la Paix”, the Drawing workshop of Arts², the higher arts school in Mons, takes over the tunnel on rue de la Croix-Rouge. This collective mural is part of the “L’Art habite la Ville” program. It turns a place of passage into a space for reflection and sharing.

The chosen theme is peace. Around twenty students express their vision there through a shared composition, guided by the Belgian artist Piet Rodriguez, known for his monumental murals. The wall then becomes a medium for expression, but also a bridge between the city, the young artists, and the people who pass through the tunnel.

As you move forward, you discover how a place marked by movement can become calmer, more open, and more symbolic. The work invites you to look at this everyday passage in a new way.

Address: Tunnel de la Croix-Rouge, 7000 Mons
en.Olivier Sonck Ivre d'histoires:
With « Ivre d’histoires », Olivier Sonck, a Belgian artist, creates a mural on the walls of the prison of Mons, rue des Barbelés. His work is linked to Mons through his studies at Arts². This work is part of the « L’Art habite la Ville » programme, and it blends image, text and memory.

The artist has long worked with printmaking, screen printing and words. Here, he draws on workshops around childhood memories, carried out with inmates and then with local residents. The result is a literary mural, full of authenticity and poetry, that gives a voice to the place and to shared stories.

Take your time to read, look and let the phrases reach you. The work changes with time and with the weather, which makes it a living presence in the city.

Address: Rue des Barbelés, 7000 Mons
en.Pierre Liebaert Je crois aux nuits:
With “Je crois aux nuits”, Pierre Liebaert, a Belgian photographer, offers an image that invites you to look at what persists in the shadows: ancient gestures, discreet presences, and forms of fragility.

His work often focuses on subjects experienced from within, over the long term. Here, he brings together fragments evoking night, wood, processions, carnival figures, and the tension between beauty and vulnerability. You are facing a photograph that links the sensory, the sacred, and the living, in a very personal language.

Address: Rue de Nimy 106, 7000 Mons.
en.Godmess Third Rua Storytelling:
"Storytelling" by Godmess and Third Rua, artists from Portugal, is part of the L'Art habite la Ville program. At Cour du Petit Marché, rue de Nimy, the mural grows out of a collaboration with children from Mons, whose drawings serve as the starting point for the final work.

The two artists work in close connection with the city and with what its residents bring to it. Godmess explores a wide variety of subjects and media. Third Rua pushes urban art toward highly present textures, almost in relief. Together, they offer a collective, living image, conceived as a story to be shared.

Address: Cour du Petit Marché, rue de Nimy, 7000 Mons.
en.Andrea Ravo Mattoni Rue de Nimy 126:
This work is part of the “L’Art habite la Ville” program. It offers an image set between light and dark, inspired by the torchlight procession and by a dialogue with great masters.

Andrea Ravo Mattoni’s work is distinguished by a direct method, without preparatory drawing, using spray on the wall. Here, the piece draws inspiration from Vélasquez, La Caravage, and John William Waterhouse, brought together in a unique composition. The result gives the wall a very particular pictorial intensity.

As you stand before this façade, you can see how a classical reference can become a contemporary urban image. The light, shadows, and silhouettes create a theatrical atmosphere that draws the eye and slows your pace.

Address: Rue de Nimy 126, 7000 Mons
en.Andrea Ravo Mattoni Charles Quint:
"Charles Quint" reinterprets an imperial portrait and brings an image drawn from classical art into public space.

Andrea Ravo Mattoni's work aims to unite the past and the present. He transfers existing works onto the wall using a technique shaped by both painting and spray. His project offers an open-air art gallery, where images once reserved for museums become visible to everyone, right in the middle of the city.

Address: Boulevard Charles Quint 18, 7000 Mons.
en.Noir Artist Don't sleep on your dream:
“Don't sleep on your dream” by Noir Artist, a Belgian artist, is part of the L'Art habite la Ville programme. On Rue de Nimy, this mural asserts a universe where advertising, pop art, baroque art, and calligraphy meet, with a very graphic energy.

Noir Artist, whose real name is Lucien Gilson, works the canvas as he does the wall, and drawing as he does the monumental mural. Here, he brings a surrealist figuration to Mons, with precise images, sometimes hyperrealistic, and a visual presence that draws the eye. You are standing before a work that plays with popular codes and reinterprets them with elegance.

Address: Rue de Nimy 121, 7000 Mons.
en.Zesar Bahamonte Le Dragon:
“Le Dragon” by Zësar Bahamonte, a Spanish artist, is part of the L'Art habite la Ville programme. On Rue du Rossignol, he reinterprets a central figure in the Mons imagination: the dragon of the Lumeçon, a creature of celebration and legend.

Zësar Bahamonte’s journey took him from Seville to Barcelona, then to Montevideo, where he developed his practice as a professional muralist. His work remains closely linked to the street, to encounters, and to urban cultures. In Mons, he also extends a connection already present with the city, in dialogue with Saint-Georges and local stories.

Address: Rue du Rossignol 14, 7000 Mons.
en.Leonidas Giannakopoulos Global City:
Here, the artist imagines a composition inspired by the Mundaneum and by the ideas of its founders. He also draws on Paul Otlet's vision of a world city that spreads knowledge and carries a spirit of cooperation. The work speaks both of the past and of the desire to dream boldly about the future.

As you look at this mural, you can see how Leonidas Giannakopoulos connects history, utopia, and the energy of street art. The title Global City sums up this ambition well: to bring Mons into dialogue with an imagination open to the world.

Address: Rue de Nimy 73, 7000 Mons.
en.Stelios Pupet Harmonizing Mons:
The artist blends figuration and geometry to create a harmonious composition. Here, he works on music and pays tribute to the Montois composer Antoine Clesse. The title Harmonizing Mons captures this idea of agreement between forms, rhythm, and local memory.

As you stop in front of this work, you can see how Stelios Pupet turns a musical subject into an urban image. The result is easy to read, yet rich in its lines and balances. The whole piece invites you to feel the city as a visual score.

Address: Rue Antoine Clesse, 7000 Mons.
en.Jana et JS Le couple de la rue Verte:
Jana & JS have been working together since 2006 and mainly use stencil techniques based on their own photographs. Their world grows out of cities, their inhabitants, façades and urban atmospheres. Here, they focus on the window as an opening onto the real world or onto an intimate, imaginary world.

The work plays with the boundary between inside and outside. You can see an almost theatrical scene, where the city enters the house and the figures seem caught in a dream. It is a mural that fits well with the surrealist spirit of Mons and with a sensitive observation of everyday life.

Address: Rue de Nimy 42, 7000 Mons.
en.Ufocinque Passeggiando nella Storia:
Ufocinque, whose real name is Matteo Capobianco, works with layering and likes to bring several levels of reading into dialogue. Here, he takes Rue des Arbalestriers, which lies along the former line of Mons's ramparts, with the nearby presence of the Tour Valenciennoise, as his starting point. The work then becomes a way of staging public space and of making the memory of the place felt.

The title Passeggiando nella Storia invites you to walk through history. You discover a mural that links the city's defensive past to a contemporary visual language, precise and open to interpretation. The whole piece presents Mons as a place where ancient traces remain alive.

Address: Rue des Arbalestriers, 7000 Mons.
en.Levalet L'homme des cavernes:
Levalet’s L'Homme des cavernes, by the French artist Levalet, is located on rue de Houdain. This work from the L'Art habite la Ville program turns the façade into a narrative set, with characters drawn in Chinese ink who interact with the architecture.

Here, you are looking at a scene suspended between realism and surrealism. Levalet creates a witty and unsettling shift, as if modern man were encountering his own origins in the public space. His work plays with several levels of meaning and with the idea of a story to be observed window by window.

Address: Rue de Houdain 1, 7000 Mons
en.Dussart Myncke True story Marche aux her:
True story by Calvin Dussart and Charles Myncke is located at the Marché aux Herbes, in Mons. This work from the L'Art habite la Ville program was created in the Drawing workshop of the École des Arts², with guidance from Djos Janssens.

The two students start from a very simple question: what do the many bricked-up windows of the city conceal? From there, they let their imagination speak and fill these openings with visual references. Comics and 1950s Hollywood film posters appear as nods to a popular visual universe.

The work plays with the idea of facade and story. You are no longer just looking at a wall; you imagine what is happening behind it. True story thus turns an urban detail into a field of fiction and shows how the city can become a medium for storytelling.

Address: Marché aux Herbes, 7000 Mons.
en.Farm Prod Rue de la Halle:
On Rue de la Halle, you will find a mural by Farm Prod, a Belgian collective. As part of the L'Art habite la Ville program, the work covers the entire façade and offers a visual journey around the Tarot, self-knowledge, and the passage of time.

At the top, Adam and Eve dominate the composition. Lower down, you can recognize figures such as The Emperor, Death, The World, and Temperance, surrounded by a plant-like setting and symbolic objects. Farm Prod invites you to see this image as a set of open signs, at once poetic and meditative.

Address: Rue de la Halle 2, 7000 Mons
en.Ilan Walbrecq Georges Cuvelier:
Rue de la Halle, this creation from the L'Art habite la Ville program is part of the Montois célèbres project. It is signed by Ilan Walbrecq, with Arts², and it highlights Georges Cuvelier, a Michelin-starred chef from Mons.

The project brings together students from the drawing workshop at Arts² around personalities from Mons. Here, the image contributes to this collective gallery of local figures and invites you to recognize a living memory of the city through the eyes of a young artist.

Address: Rue de la Halle 42, 7000 Mons
en.Hell'O Rue de la Halle:
Rue de la Halle, Hell'O, the Belgian duo made up of Jérôme Meynen and Antoine Detaille, presents a work in the L'Art habite la Ville program. Here, the wall becomes a composition in sixteen panels that brings pastel colors, delicate drawing and architecture into dialogue.

The duo, coming from graffiti, works with motifs, imaginary beings and forms somewhere between figuration and abstraction. You can read a surreal and soothing universe here, where the eye plays a central role. The fragments fit together without imposing a single reading, letting your gaze wander freely.

Address: Rue de la Halle 5, 7000 Mons
en.Cedric Le Borgne La riviere:
At the Marché-aux-Poissons, you discover La Rivière by Cédric Le Borgne, a French artist. This work, part of the L'Art habite la Ville programme, features two giant koi carp that seem to swim through the air, lit from within.

The installation catches your eye and brings you back to your own scale in the face of nature. Cédric Le Borgne works with public space, encounters and sharing, and this piece gives Mons a poetic image, suspended between reality and imagination.

Address: Marché aux Poissons, 7000 Mons
en.Taquen Bouquet of memory and hope:
Here is “Bouquet of memory and hope” by Taquen, a Spanish artist, in rue des Chartriers. This work is part of the L'Art habite la Ville programme, and it invites you to see the poppy as a symbol of remembrance and poetry.

With this painting, Taquen reminds us that simple images can carry a heavy memory. He transforms a place marked by a painful past into a bouquet that also speaks of tenderness and hope.

Where bombs once fell, poppies now grow. Address: Rue des Chartriers 2, 7000 Mons.
en.Dussart Myncke True story Croix Place:
Here is “True story” by Calvin Dussart and Charles Myncke, artists from Belgium, at Croix-Place, rue de Houdain. This work is part of the L'Art habite la Ville program, and it fits into the urban landscape of Mons with a title that immediately grabs your attention.

The two artists here give the street a stronger presence. The name “True story” suggests a scene to be read like a narrative, somewhere between reality and the artist’s gaze, without revealing too much and leaving room for your own interpretation.

Address: Croix-Place, 7000 Mons.
en.Eva Badalamenti Louis Buisseret:
Here is “Louis Buisseret” by Eva Badalamenti, created with Arts², rue des Sœurs Noires. This work is part of the L'Art habite la Ville programme, within the “Montois célèbres” project, where students from Arts² turn personalities linked to Mons into images.

Here, the portrait pays tribute to Louis Buisseret. The idea behind the project is to reveal, along the walls, a series of figures from Mons chosen to tell the city’s story in a different way, through an artistic and collective approach.

Eva Badalamenti’s work is thus part of an open-air gallery. You are invited to look up and recognize, in the public space, a local memory that takes shape every day.

Address: Rue des Sœurs Noires 19, 7000 Mons.
en.Thomas Istasse La lune de Malapert:
Here is “The Moon of Malapert” by Thomas Istasse, created with Arts², at the corner of rue de la Trouille and rue Malapert. This work is part of the L'Art habite la Ville program, in the “Famous Montois” series, which brings the city into dialogue with its notable figures.

Here, the name Malapert refers to Charles Malapert, a researcher and mathematician from Mons who observed the sky. The work also reminds us that a name can live in several places, in a street in Mons as well as in a lunar crater.

Thomas Istasse offers you a gaze turned upward, with an image bathed in light. It is a poetic way of linking the Montois land to space, while remaining rooted in local memory.

Address: Rue Malapert, 7000 Mons.
en.Andrea Buglisi La Gayole:
Here is “La Gayole” by Andrea Buglisi, an Italian artist, on rue des Arquebusiers. This work is part of the L'Art habite la Ville program, and it revisits the tradition of the “Gayoles” through the artist’s own visual language.

Andrea Buglisi likes to create a visual trap. He first draws you in with appealing colors, then slips in a more unsettling message, with a touch of irony. Here, he imagines the building as a birdcage, but an open one, where the birds remain free.

The work thus brings together nature, tradition, and modernity. It turns the wall into a striking image that also speaks about families, work, and a popular memory reinterpreted today.

Address: Rue des Arquebusiers 3, 7000 Mons.
en.Oli-B L'escapade:
In the Gustave Jacobs garden, you can see “L'escapade” by Oli-B, a Brussels artist, as part of the L'Art habite la Ville program. His world plays with abstract and figurative shapes, bright colors, and a sense of movement. Here, the work invites you to step into a softer, brighter world.

Oli-B likes large public spaces and city life. On this wall, he offers an optimistic vision where dreamlike imagery blends with harmony. You can take a moment to notice how the shapes seem to breathe with the garden.

Address: Jardin Gustave Jacobs, 7000 Mons
en.Blancbec Le monstrueux:
Rue d'Havré 95, you discover « Le monstrueux » by Blancbec, a work from the L'Art habite la Ville program. In collaboration with the neighbours, the artist transformed this wall into a scene populated by imaginary animals and plants. The whole creates a living world, both playful and surprising.

Blancbec, a Belgian artist, builds here a very recognizable universe. His geometric shapes and bright colour palette come from graffiti and from his work around posters and characters. The bird, and then other figures, gradually gave birth to a distinctive style.

As you move along the street, you can see how this mural enters into dialogue with the neighbourhood. It brings a strong presence to the public space and shows how a wall can become a place of shared history.

Address: Rue d'Havré 95, 7000 Mons
en.Nevercrew Dissipation:
On Rue à Degrés, you will discover « Dissipation » by Nevercrew, a duo of contemporary Swiss artists, as part of L'Art habite la Ville. Christian Rebecchi and Pablo Togni often create monumental, precise, and committed murals. Here, they choose to go against the street’s name.

The work addresses climate change and invites reflection on our relationship with the world. Another special feature of this project is that, for the first time, Nevercrew worked directly on the ground of the rue à degrés. The gesture is strong and direct, and the location fully contributes to the reading of the work.

As you stand in front of the mural, you can feel this dialogue between the subject and the space. The whole piece combines commitment, technique, and a взгляд on human and environmental issues.

Address: Rue à Degrés, 7000 Mons
en.Duek Eldorado:
At 19 Rue des Fripiers, you discover “Eldorado” by Duek, a work in the L'Art habite la Ville programme. The artist, originally from Spain, takes inspiration here from Mexico and its culture, which is very closely linked to nature and mysticism. The mural features women, flowers, and a Quetzal, the country’s emblematic bird.

The whole composition evokes beauty, delicacy, and the strength of life all at once. Natural elements are omnipresent and recall the deep connection between human beings and their environment. This highly colorful composition invites you to see the wall as a visual story.

As you pass by this mural, you may notice how the shapes and symbols respond to one another. Here, Duek creates a rich universe where nature and culture move forward together.

Address: Rue des Fripiers 19, 7000 Mons
en.Poni Grand Rue:
At Grand'Rue 8, you will discover a mural by Poni, a Mexican artist, as part of the L'Art habite la Ville programme. Poni, also known as Hilda Palafox, is making her first appearance in Belgium here. Her style combines fluidity, simplicity and a very poetic aesthetic.

The artist often draws women without pupils, inviting the viewer to travel. On this wall in Mons, she places a female figure with the city hill in the background. The result is calm, elegant, and very open to the imagination.

As you look at the mural, you can appreciate the softness of the lines and the space left to the landscape. Poni transforms the façade into a silent scene, yet one full of presence.

Address: Grand'Rue 8, 7000 Mons
en.Paul Segard Ma ville s'endort:
With “Ma ville s’endort”, Paul Segard, an artist from Belgium, chooses a calm and poetic atmosphere in the Passage du Centre, rue Grand'rue. This work from the L’Art habite la Ville program is inspired by Mons’s heritage and by the charm of the city center, which the artist particularly loves.

The mural plays with pastel colors and a simple scene: a sleeping figure watches over the city. The image evokes the attachment of the people of Mons to their living environment, with a feeling of softness and intimacy. You are looking at a work that invites you to slow down and see Mons differently.

Address: Passage du Centre, 7000 Mons.
en.Dulk The battle:
With “The battle”, Dulk, an artist from Spain, brings a very lively imagination to Rue des Capucins. This work from the L’Art habite la Ville program reflects his practice across urban art, mural painting and other forms of expression, with a strong attention to color and storytelling.

The mural invites you into a dream world filled with animals and natural landscapes. Here, Dulk also defends, discreetly but powerfully, ecosystems and the most vulnerable species. Here you discover an image that aims to move you as much as to take you on a journey.

Address: Rue des Capucins 13, 7000 Mons.
en.Celeste Gangolphe Mille et une feuille:
In “Mille et une feuille”, Céleste Gangolphe, an artist from France, transforms Rue des Capucins into a plant-inspired setting. This work from the L’Art habite la Ville program brings a breath of nature to Mons, highly visible in a mineral city, and catches the eye as soon as you walk down the street.

The artist likes to combine drawing, painting, collage and patterns. Here, she creates figures inspired by the Doudou, the Hommes et les Enfants de Feuilles, as if hidden in ivy taking over the wall. The mural also speaks of transmission and the link between humans and nature, at the heart of Mons folklore.

Address: Rue des Capucins 40, 7000 Mons.
en.Nean Cybele et Poliade:
In « Cybèle et Poliade », NEAN, an artist from Belgium, pays tribute to two figures present in the arena of the fight known as Lumeçon, on rue des Capucins. This work from the L’Art habite la Ville program is part of a reflection dear to the artist: time, memories, and the way they transform.

The mural is not merely decorative. It pays tribute to a living folklore, capable of evolving and reinventing itself. The wall here becomes an ideal support, with its marks, layers and visible history. You are looking at a work that links personal memory and collective memory.

Address: Rue des Capucins 37, 7000 Mons.
en.Arts2 Roland de Lassus:
With “Roland de Lassus,” the students of Arts² are highlighting a famous person from Mons. This work from the L’Art habite la Ville program can be discovered on rue des 5 visages, and it brings local memory into public space.

Here you are looking at a collective creation, designed by the students of Arts² in Belgium. The portrait becomes a nod to Roland de Lassus and reminds us how the figures of Mons continue to inspire contemporary art.

As you walk along the street, take the time to look at the composition and its relationship with the wall. The work accompanies you along the route and invites you to connect heritage, the city, and contemporary creation.

Address: Rue des 5 visages, 7000 Mons.
en.10eme ARTE L'envol des ballons:
With « L’envol des ballons », 10ème ARTE, an artist duo from Spain and Italy working in Brussels, installs a mural full of movement on rue de l’Athénée. This work from the L’Art habite la Ville programme draws inspiration from Mons folklore and from the enthusiasm surrounding the so-called Lumeçon battle.

Your gaze first discovers gathered faces, varied and expressive, then balloons rising toward the sky. The image creates a link between the crowd on the Grand-Place and this shared moment of emotion. The gesture is simple, but it speaks of freedom, lightness, and collective energy.

Address: Rue de l'Athénée 3, 7000 Mons.
en.Andrea Ravo Mattoni Sainte Waudru et ses:
With “Sainte Waudru et ses filles visitant les prisonniers”, Andrea Ravo Mattoni, an artist from Italy, brings a classical image into the city. This work from the L’Art habite la Ville programme can be discovered on rue du Chapitre, directly linked to the nearby Collégiale.

The artist takes up a scene associated with Antoine Van Ysendick and transposes it onto a large wall visible to everyone. He combines an academic gesture with spray paint to create a dialogue between past and present, and to open art up to public space.

Looking at this mural, you rediscover Sainte Waudru, a powerful figure in Mons, in a contemporary reading. The whole piece invites you to look up and make the connection between the city’s heritage and today’s creation.

Address: Rue du Chapitre, 2, 7000 Mons.
en.Filip Gilissen Spread your wings:
With “Spread your wings”, Filip Gilissen, an artist from Belgium, offers an installation that immediately catches the eye. This work from the L’Art habite la Ville programme is located on Square Saint-Germain, in an open space where art meets everyday life.

The installation evokes wings and an upward momentum, with a bright, festive touch. It also echoes the Collégiale Sainte-Waudru, visible in the landscape, and turns the place into a cheerful, symbolic stop.

You can stand in front of the work and let the perspective interact with the monument in the background. Here, urban art creates a simple, visual, and shareable moment in the heart of the city.

Address: Square Saint-Germain, 7000 Mons.
en.Ana Langeheldt Alegoria de santa Valdetr:
With “Alegoría de Santa Valdetrudis,” Ana Langeheldt, an artist from Spain, puts her style at the service of Mons folklore. This work from the L’Art habite la Ville program can be discovered on Rampe Sainte-Waudru, in a place rich in symbolism for the city.

The artist, also known as Lahe178, reinterprets the ascent of the Car d’Or here with an urban and contemporary perspective. She connects her practice of urban art in Andalusia with a local tradition that is deeply rooted in Mons.

As you stop in front of the work, you can see how a popular celebration can become material for creation. The wall then becomes a living surface, between collective memory and contemporary expression.

Address: Rampe Sainte-Waudru, 4, 7000 Mons.
en.Rachelle Celiane Santerre Jacques Du Bro:
With “Jacques Du Broeucq”, Rachelle & Céliane Santerre, in partnership with Arts², pay tribute to a major figure from Mons. This work from the L’Art habite la Ville program can be found on rue du Chapitre, as part of the “Montois célèbres” project.

The work highlights the architect and sculptor Jacques Du Broeucq, and is part of a series created by students from the drawing workshop at Arts². The idea is simple: to bring into the city personalities who have shaped Mons, and make them visible as you turn a corner.

By looking at this creation, you can see how a tribute can become a presence in public space. The work connects the Montois past with a contemporary graphic vision, accessible to everyone.

Address: Rue du Chapitre, 3, 7000 Mons.
en.Margaux Del Vecchio Anto Carte:
On Roosevelt Square, Margaux Del Vecchio presents “Montois célèbres : Anto Carte”. The work portrays the Mons-born painter Anto Carte, and it is part of the “L’Art habite la Ville” programme, which brings art into your walk through Mons.

Here, the portrait becomes a nod to local memory. You are standing in front of a work by Margaux Del Vecchio, in a series that highlights notable people from Mons and enters into dialogue with the city along the route.

Address: Square Roosevelt, 5 - 7000 Mons
en.Projeto Ruido Le temps:
On Rue Claude de Bettignies, Projeto Ruído presents « Le temps ». This Portuguese project brings together Draw, Frederico Soares Campos, and Contra, Rodrigo Guinea Gonçalves. Their work blends graffiti, figurative forms, abstraction, and color into a piece designed for urban space.

Here, the street becomes a space for dialogue. The work accompanies your walk toward the Musée Duesberg and plays with the idea of time, while revealing the encounter between very different graphic languages. It is a creation from the « L’Art habite la Ville » program.

Address: Rue Claude de Bettignies, 19 - 7000 Mons
en.Robert Montgomery Invisible graffiti of:
At Place Léopold, Robert Montgomery presents “Invisible graffiti of love.” The artist, from the United Kingdom, uses words here to bring a light, poetic presence into public space. The work is part of the “L’Art habite la Ville” programme.

The title invites you to look up and slow down. In the rhythm of the square, this creation turns a simple walk-through into a moment of reading and attention. It adds an intimate voice to the Mons landscape, while remaining in keeping with the sobriety of the place.

Address: Place Léopold, 7000 Mons
en.Momo Rue Cantimpret:
On Rue Cantimpré, MOMO creates a mural made of striped blocks of colour. The artist, who comes from the United States, is known for graphic interventions that draw new urban maps, from the smallest gesture to the monumental mural. Here, he is taking part in the “L’Art habite la Ville” programme.

The composition catches the eye with its rhythm and contrasts. It gives the street a special energy and extends the movement of the route into the public space. The wall becomes a visual landmark that accompanies your walk through Mons.

Address: Rue Cantimpré 14, 7000 Mons
en.Zmogk The elements:
On Rue des Canonniers, Zmogk presents “The elements”. The artist, who comes from Russia, has developed a lively and highly recognizable style, with dynamic compositions full of color and sensitivity. Here, his work is part of the “L’Art habite la Ville” program.

The artwork brings fire to the street, just steps from Place Nervienne. It speaks to a place known for hosting the Feux de la Saint-Jean, and gives the wall a vibrant presence, almost in motion. The eye then follows the shapes like an energy flowing through the street.

Address: Rue des Cannoniers 18, 7000 Mons
en.Arkane Lalie:
You are standing in front of “Lalie” by Arkane, a work in the L’Art habite la Ville program, on rue de Bertaimont in Mons. Arkane is a multidisciplinary artist originally from France. Here, he offers a sensitive image, with a subtle narrative, where light and framing create a very embodied atmosphere.

The subject enters into dialogue with the folklore of the Messine district. The artist draws inspiration from the Giants of Messines and imagines what these figures would look like if they became real people. It is a way of linking local history to a very contemporary presence, right in the heart of the city.

This mural is part of the “L’Art habite la Ville” walk and helps make Mons an open-air art space. Address: Rue de Bertaimont 55, 7000 Mons.
en.Tris Horizon:
You are discovering “Horizon” by Tris, a work in the L’Art habite la Ville programme, on boulevard Sainctelette in Mons. Tris is a French artist who has been based in London since 2022. His work mixes several techniques and creates a universe between comics and realism, with an atmosphere that recalls cinema.

Here, he draws inspiration from the street itself and its history. Boulevard Sainctelette follows the former line of the ramparts and the city gates. The artist takes up the theme of gates on this building with blind windows, turning the architecture into an image open to the imagination.

This mural is part of the “L’Art habite la Ville” route and invites you to look differently at a place of passage. Address: Boulevard Sainctelette 62, 7000 Mons.
en.Dourone Boulevard Sainctelette:
You are discovering a mural by Dourone, a work in the L’Art habite la Ville programme, on Boulevard Sainctelette in Mons. Dourone brings together Fabio Lopez and Elodie Arshak, two artists from Spain. Their approach always places people at the centre, with a strong connection to the local residents and to the context of the place.

Here, they draw inspiration from the solidarity in the city and from the history of the Ducasse de Mons. For them, the Doudou perfectly represents this solidarity in Mons, across generations and shared by everyone. They also mention UNESCO’s recognition of this festival as a masterpiece of the oral and intangible heritage of humanity.

This work is part of the “L’Art habite la Ville” route and gives Boulevard Sainctelette a very lively presence. Address: Boulevard Sainctelette 76, 7000 Mons.
en.Nadege Dauvergne Place du Beguinage:
You are standing in front of a mural by Nadège Dauvergne, a work from the L’Art habite la Ville program, on Place du Béguinage in Mons. The artist is French. Here, she draws inspiration from the Sunday market that has enlivened this neighborhood for decades, and she builds her image around the idea of abundance.

Her work also echoes 17th-century still lifes, especially those by Joris Van Son. Nadège Dauvergne works from classical painting, then changes scale to create large monumental murals. This shift from canvas to public space offers a new reading of everyday life.

This work shows you how art can enter into dialogue with the habits of a neighborhood while remaining very much alive. It is part of the route “L’Art habite la Ville”. Address: Place du Béguinage 13, 7000 Mons.
en.Daniel Eime Resistance:
You are discovering “Résistance” by Daniel Eime, a work from the L’Art habite la Ville program, on boulevard Sainctelette in Mons. Daniel Eime is an artist originally from Portugal. He has been living from his art since 2011 and started out very young on the street, experimenting with graffiti.

His style is recognizable by the use of stencils, a technique he uses in all his creations. He combines them with pop elements, realism, precise details, and colorful geometric patterns. This combination gives the work a very distinctive visual power. Here, Daniel Eime pays tribute to Marguerite Bervoets.

This mural is part of the “L’Art habite la Ville” trail and gives boulevard Sainctelette a sense of memory and presence. Address: Boulevard Sainctelette 133, 7000 Mons.
en.Portes du Theatre Royal:
Look at the porch here on the Grand-Place, at the corner of rue Neuve. Charles Sury, the city's architect, built this neoclassical theater between 1841 and 1843. It was then called the Grand Théâtre; the public first entered it on October 18, 1843. Three grilles close off the passage, between Ionic columns. Ph.-J. Hoyois, a blacksmith, crafted them. Émile-Joseph Hoyaux, a sculptor from Mons barely twenty years old, placed the faces there in 1846. At the pediment: the attributes of stage and music.

In the 20th century, the building no longer provided enough protection. Work began in 1938: the overly worn auditorium disappeared, and Govaerts and Van Varenberg designed a new one, inaugurated on October 4, 1948. To accommodate a safer, more convenient interior staircase, the original grilles were preserved — but they were cut in height. They have changed in size, not in place.

Address: Grand-Place, 7000 Mons.
en.Blasons muets:
You are in front of a Gothic house at 8 Miroir Street. Blue stone and plastered brick: the 16th-century Mons, still legible despite the centuries. David Longhet, who will become an alderman in 1551, had it built; the date 1545 is engraved above the door on a plaque.

This is where the mute coats of arms are found. Two shields frame the dated band, but their fields are empty: no arms, no figures. In heraldry, a mute shield is still waiting for its identity or keeps it silent. The slightly compressed lintel features a bracketed molding; the central finial rests on the plaque. A sign reminds us that this is a Gothic house.

Next, raise your gaze to the facade. Three levels, three bays. On the lower floors, three-lobed arches project in corbel, resting on prismatic corbels.
